extracted.intended_audience: editors, proofreaders, authors, and University of Chicago Press / publishing staff
extracted.subtask_description: A university-press style manual giving detailed typographical and editorial rules (capitalization, punctuation, italics, quotations, indexing, tabular work, technical terms, etc.) intended to govern publications printed by a press and to guide editors/proofreaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: proper nouns and adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper nouns and adjectives should be capitalized (examples: George, America, North America, Englishman; Elizabethan, French).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize verbs derived from proper names having a specialized meaning (to boycott, to fletcherize, to pasteurize) nor such words as volt, ampere, angstrom, farad, watt, henry, ohm, coulomb when used in their special scientific or trade significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize: epithets used as substitutes for proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize epithets used as substitutes for proper names or affixed to a name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Pretender, Bloody Mary, Richard the Lion-hearted, Alexander the Great.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize particles in French names conditionally; treatment of Van/von
rubrics_metrics.description: Particles in French names ('le', 'la', 'de', 'du') are capitalized when not preceded by a Christian name or title; do not capitalize them when preceded by such name or title. Capitalize 'Van' in Dutch names; do not capitalize 'von' in German names unless it begins a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Le Bossu, La Rochelle, De Coligny, Du Maurier (but: Rene le Bossu; Gaspard de Coligny). Stephen Van Rensselaer; Hugo von Martius. Note exceptions due to personal preference (Henry van Dyke, J. H. van't Hoff).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize generic terms forming part of geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic geographical terms that form an integral part of a name are capitalized (e.g., Atlantic Ocean, Gulf of Mexico, Mississippi River).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize when the generic term is merely descriptive (the river Elbe, the desert of Sahara). The manual gives lists of generic terms that are capitalized when immediately following the name, or before/after the name, with singular/plural rules (Archipelago, Hill, Island, Bay, Lake, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize adjectives and nouns distinguishing definite regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives and nouns used singly or in conjunction to distinguish definite regions or used with recognized geographical terms should be capitalized (Old World, Western Hemisphere, North Pole, the Levant, the North, Middle West).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not as a rule capitalize adjectives derived from such names or nouns simply designating direction (oriental customs, the southern states). To mark world-wide application, capitalize (Eastern peoples; Western nations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize generic terms for political divisions when integral to name
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic terms for political divisions are capitalized when they are an organic part of the name (Holy Roman Empire, French Republic, United Kingdom, Cook County).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used with 'of' as integral (Department of the Lakes) or when used singly as an accepted designation (the Union, the States) capitalize. Do not capitalize when standing alone or used generically (the empire, the state; empire of Russia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize numbered political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbered political divisions are capitalized: Eleventh Congressional District, First Ward, Second Precinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule references for numbering conventions (also cf. 100).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of thoroughfares, parks, squares, blocks, buildings, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of streets, parks, squares, blocks, buildings, and similar specific places are capitalized (Drexel Avenue, Lincoln Park, Trafalgar Square, Monadnock Block).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general designations like 'courthouse', 'post-office', 'library' except when forming part of a proper name (e.g., Chicago Public Library).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of political parties, religious denominations, schools, movements and adherents
rubrics_metrics.description: The names of parties, denominations, sects, philosophical/literary/artistic schools, and their adherents are capitalized (Republican, Evangelical Lutheran, Catholic, Epicurean, Stoic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize these words or their derivatives when used in a general sense of trend, spirit, or attitude (republican form of government, socialism as an economic panacea, puritanical ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of monastic orders and members
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of monastic orders and their members are capitalized (Black Friars, Dominican, Jesuit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No extended exceptions given beyond examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize proper (official) titles of organizations and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Official titles of social, religious, educational, political, commercial, and industrial organizations and institutions are capitalized (Union League Club, Smithsonian Institution, State University of Iowa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic terms when used to designate a class or when standing alone (young people's societies, the club) unless used consistently in place of the true name or to avoid ambiguity (He joined the Hall [Tammany]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize legislative, judiciary, administrative bodies & departments when specifically applied
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of legislative, judicial, and administrative bodies and departments and their branches are capitalized when specifically applied (Congress, Parliament, Supreme Court of the United States, Department of the Interior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general, paraphrastic, or incomplete designations (the national assembly, the legislature of the state, the council).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize ordinals in certain institutional/historical sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinals used to designate Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, names of regiments, etc., are capitalized (the Eighteenth Dynasty, the Fifty-third Congress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with names like 'Ming dynasty' which are lower-case for 'dynasty'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize commonly accepted appellations for epochs, language periods, geological ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of historical epochs, literary language periods, geological ages and strata are capitalized as standard appellations (Renaissance, Reformation, Pleistocene, Christian Era).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize informal adjectives (early Algonkian, late Permian). Capitalize 'Age' only when failure to do so would be ambiguous (Stone Age vs. neolithic age).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of important events
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of significant historical events are capitalized (Thirty Years' War, Revolutionary War, Battle of Gettysburg, Louisiana Purchase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate conventions for wars, purchases, and treaties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names of political alliances and historically significant terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Political alliances and terms with acquired historical significance are capitalized (Protestant League, Holy Alliance, the Roses, the Roundheads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related rule for parties and movements (9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize conventions, congresses, expositions, official gatherings
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of conventions, congresses, expositions and similar gatherings are capitalized (Council of Nicaea, Westminster Assembly, Chicago World's Fair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include ordinal numbering when part of formal title (Fifteenth International Congress of Criminology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize titles of specific treaties, acts, laws, bills and juridical instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific formal titles of treaties, acts, laws and juridical instruments are capitalized (Treaty of Verdun, Magna Charta, Fourteenth Amendment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize bills that have not become laws nor such treaties or laws when cited otherwise than under their formal titles (treaty at Versailles, Food bill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize creeds and confessions of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of creeds and confessions are capitalized (Apostles' Creed, Nicene Creed, Augsburg Confession).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjectival or descriptive modifiers like 'ante-Nicene' may be lower-case as noted; see cross-references (203,208).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize civic holidays and ecclesiastical feast/fast days
rubrics_metrics.description: Civic holidays and ecclesiastical feast or fast days are capitalized (Fourth of July, Labor Day, Easter, Passover).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common abbreviations like 'the Fourth' are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize official titles of honor and degrees preceding or following names
rubrics_metrics.description: Official titles of honor, respect, nobility preceding the name and academic degrees following the name are capitalized (Queen Victoria, Rear-Admiral Dewey, Timothy Dwight, D.D., LL.D.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize such titles when they follow the name (Woodrow Wilson, president of the United States) or when standing alone in a generic sense (the archbishop when not referring to the incumbent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Set without spaces: abbreviations like Ph.D., M.P., F.R.G.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations comprised of initials for degrees and honors and designations of celestial objects should be set without spaces between letters (Ph.D., M.P., F.R.G.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also treatment of A.M./P.M./B.C./A.D. (rule 52) and other abbreviation spacing rules (22,103,106).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize single-letter abbreviations except measurement units and minor subdivisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations consisting of one letter are capitalized except in the case of units of measurement and minor literary subdivisions (R.V., F., C., A) but not p., l., n., etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: R.V. (Revised Version), F. (Fahrenheit), C. (centigrade), A (angstrom units).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize nouns/adjectives designating the Supreme Being or Trinity and pronouns referring to Them
rubrics_metrics.description: Nouns and adjectives used to designate the Supreme Being or the Christian Trinity, and pronouns referring to Them, are capitalized (the Almighty, Father, Son, Holy Ghost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize derivatives like father's (God's) fatherhood, messiahship, messianic where cited as derivations; exception if closely preceded/followed by a distinctive name or to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize words with an acquired, limited, or special meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Words that have taken on an acquired, limited, or special meaning are capitalized (the Doctor's degree, a report of the Master, a Bachelor's hood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize the generic terms (the doctorate, a master in chancery) where the explanatory words remove the necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize personified abstract terms like 'Nature'
rubrics_metrics.description: Personified abstract terms are capitalized ("Nature wields her scepter mercilessly").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use capitalization when personification is clearly intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize 'Father' and 'Reformers' in ecclesiastical-historical senses when ambiguity requires
rubrics_metrics.description: Use capitalization for 'Father' meaning church Father and 'Reformers' for Reformation leaders when needed to avoid ambiguity (the Fathers, the Reformers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower-case when context makes the reference generic (the church reformers of the fifteenth century).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize 'church' in proper cited institutional titles or when part of edifice names
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'church' is capitalized in properly cited titles of nationally organized bodies or when it is part of a building's specific name (Church of Rome, First Methodist Church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize 'church' when standing alone in universal, national, or local senses (the church = organized Christianity) except in exceptional rhetorical emphasis contrasting Church and State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names for the Bible and other sacred books
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of the Bible and other sacred works are capitalized (Holy Scriptures, Koran, Vedas, Mishna).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize adjectives derived from these nouns (biblical, scriptural, koranic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize versions and editions of the Bible
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of Bible versions and editions are capitalized (King James's Version, Authorized Version, Revised Version).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include common abbreviations (A.V., R.V.) without spaces as per rules on abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize books and divisions of the Bible and other sacred works
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of biblical books and their divisions are capitalized (Old Testament, Exodus, Psalms, Epistle to the Romans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize the common nouns 'book', 'gospel', 'epistle', 'psalm' when used generically (the five books of Moses, the gospels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize biblical parables where specific name is used
rubrics_metrics.description: Properly titled biblical parables are capitalized (the parable of the Prodigal Son).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short rule — treat named parables as titled entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize miscellaneous sacred-history terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Miscellaneous terms with special scriptural/historical import are capitalized (Last Supper, Eucharist, the Passion, the Golden Rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when specific traditional labels apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize the first word of a sentence and first word of each line in English poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Always capitalize the first word of a sentence; in English poetry capitalize the first word of each line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Greek and Latin poetry capitalize only the first word of a paragraph, not each line. Examples of both provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize first word after colon only when introducing an independent sentence or complete passage
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word after a colon only when it introduces a complete sentence or passage that stands independently (as in quotations or summarizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize when the quotation is immediately connected with the preceding clause or when the colon implies 'namely' followed by a brief dependent phrase. Examples: correct and incorrect usages shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize first words in enumerations when items are independent clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: In enumerations where an item contains two or more distinct clauses separated by semicolon, colon, or period, capitalize the first word of each such section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrasts: when items are independent vs. when they are dependent upon the leading term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize nouns followed by numerals indicating order in a sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize nouns followed by numerals indicating order (Room 16, Vol. I, Act I, Book II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize minor subdivisions of publications like 'sec 4', 'scene i', 'chap. 2 (ii)'. See cross-reference to rule for minor subdivisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize first word of cited speech or thought in direct discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: The first word of a cited speech or thought in direct discourse is capitalized whether preceded by colon or comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: On leaving he remarked: 'Never shall I forget this day.' With the words, 'Never shall I forget this day,' he departed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize first words following 'WHEREAS' and 'Resolved' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In formal resolutions set the first words following WHEREAS and Resolved in capitals (e.g., WHEREAS, It has pleased God...; Resolved, That...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting conventions: NOTE should be followed by period and dash in notes; SECTION used to introduce numbered paragraphs in constitutions/by-laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize exclamations 'O' and 'Oh'
rubrics_metrics.description: The vocative exclamations 'O' and 'Oh' are capitalized ("O Lord!", "Oh, that I were home again!").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See punctuation rules (117) for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize principal words in English titles of publications and divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: All principal words in English titles of publications, and their divisions, and in subjects of lectures/toasts, should be capitalized (The Men Who Made the Nation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cap-and-small-cap and italic center-heads when possible. Note: Botanical Gazette practice differs (capitalize only first words and proper names) and may be followed for general bibliographies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization rules for foreign-language titles
rubrics_metrics.description: For foreign titles: Latin—capitalize proper nouns and derived adjectives; French/Italian/Spanish/Swedish/Norwegian—capitalize proper nouns but not adjectives derived therefrom; German/Danish—capitalize all nouns (but not adjectives); Dutch—capitalize all nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for each language (De amicitia; Histoire de la literature francaise; Geschichte des deutschen Feudalwesens; Geschiedenis der Nederlandsche Taal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat the definite article as part of newspaper/magazine titles
rubrics_metrics.description: When mentioning newspapers or magazines do not, as a rule, treat the definite article as part of the title (the Chicago Tribune, the School Review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions are allowed but the usual practice is to omit the article from the title proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize titles of ancient manuscripts (MS, MSS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of ancient manuscripts are capitalized (Codex Bernensis, Cod. Canonicianus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule cross-references around biblical and manuscript citation conventions (60).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize nouns in hyphenated titles when they are nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with main words capitalized, all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds are capitalized (Twentieth-Century Progress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize hyphenated components that are not nouns (Fifty-first Street). Side-heads: only capitalize first word and proper nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize scientific (Latin) names for taxonomic divisions; handle species names with discipline-specific exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: In botanical, geological, zoological, and paleontological contexts, scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera are capitalized, but their English derivatives are not (Cotylosauria vs. cotylosaurs). Species names: capitalize if derived from persons or from generic names in some fields; in geological and medical matter species names are never capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felidae (family) but 'felids' in English; Felis leo, Rosa Carolina, but geological species Pterygomatopus schmidti. See rule 71 for italics usage on species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes are capitalized (Kafir, Negro, Makassar, Celestials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historically and ethnographically appropriate forms; consult related entries for indexing conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical capitalization conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In astronomical works, capitalize names of planets, stars, and groups of stars (Saturn, Ursa Major, the Milky Way), but not common nouns like 'sun', 'earth', 'moon', 'stars'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also capitalize designations of celestial objects in well-known catalogues (M 13, N.G.C. 6165, Lalande 5761).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize official University divisions, departments, officers and course names in official work
rubrics_metrics.description: Within official publications of the University of Chicago, capitalize divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study (the School of Education, Department of Anthropology, Board of Trustees, Dean of the Faculties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific internal conventions: allowable short forms in parentheses (the School, the Department). Use capitals & small caps for certain dateline/signature formats (rule 50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use capitals and small capitals for dateline/salutatory/signature lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Set names of town and state in the date line, the salutatory phrase at the beginning of letters, and the signature/residence in capitals and small capitals (e.g., CHICAGO, ILL.; MY DEAR MR. SMITH:; CHARLES W. SCOTT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting notes: date set to the right with one em indention; signatures set to the right in same type as body; address lines centered and in caps & small caps; date in caps and lower case centered under address lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'WHEREAS', 'NOTE', and 'SECTION' in caps for formal documents
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions use 'WHEREAS' in caps; in notes use 'NOTE' (followed by period and dash); in constitutions/by-laws use 'SECTION' to introduce paragraphs and follow it by a number. Abbreviate 'SECTION' except on first occurrence (SEC. 2...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show conventional placement and abbreviation practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set A.M., P.M., B.C., and A.D. in small capitals without spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A.M., P.M., B.C., and A.D. should be set in small capitals and without spaces between letters (11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references: see rules 22, 103, 106 for related abbreviation spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lower-case initial letter for common words originally proper names where origin is obscured
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of common usage that were originally proper names (and whose origin has become obscured) and their derivatives should use a small initial letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the opening of rule 53; examples and full scope continue in subsequent text (truncated here). Typically applies to words like 'damask' from Damascus, 'champagne' from Champagne, etc., when fully lexicalized.
